knowledge_checks.title: Active Recall: 5.1.8
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Which statement correctly describes how Empirical Bayes obtains structural parameters differently from a fully specified Bayesian prior and names the premium derived?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: EB estimates overall mean and process variance components from collective experience, then forms credibility premium. Same assumptions as fully Bayesian is incorrect.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Estimate structurals from collective data; premium Ẑ $\bar{X}$ + (1-Ẑ) $\hat{\mu}$.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Treating EB as identical assumptions or single-claim update.

choices.label: Empirical Bayes estimates structural parameters from collective data rather than treating them as fully specified by a prior alone. The credibility premium Ẑ times $\bar{X}$ + (1 minus Ẑ) times $\mu$-hat follows after plugging estimated structural parameters into the credibility formula.
Empirical Bayes and fully Bayesian credibility always use identical assumptions for structural parameters.
Empirical Bayes obtains the premium only by applying Bayes' theorem to a single claim; collective data never enter.
Empirical Bayes means choosing Z = 1 always because data estimate full credibility automatically.

knowledge_checks.title: Checkpoint: 5.1.8
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Under Empirical Bayes, structural parameters are estimated from collective data: $\hat{\mu}$ = 900 and $\hat{k}$ = 6. A risk has $n = 3$ years with $\bar{X}$ = 1200. Enter the EB credibility premium $P = \hat{Z}\bar{X} + (1 - \hat{Z})\hat{\mu}$ where $\hat{Z} = n/(n+\hat{k})$.
knowledge_checks.body: Compute $\hat{Z}$ from $n$ and $\hat{k}$, then evaluate the EB credibility premium.
knowledge_checks.explanation: $\hat{Z} = 3/(3+6) = 1/3$, so $P = (1/3)\times 1200 + (2/3)\times 900 = 1000$. Structurals $\hat{\mu}$ and $\hat{k}$ are collective estimates, not a fully specified prior.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Using $\hat{Z} = \hat{k}/(n+\hat{k}) = 2/3$ (swapping weights) to get 1100, or taking full credibility $P = 1200$.

worked_example.title: Empirical Bayes premium with estimated structurals
worked_example.problem_statement: Under Empirical Bayes, structural parameters are estimated from collective data: $\hat{\mu}$ = £900 and $\hat{k}$ = 6. A risk has n = 3 years with $\bar{X}$ = £1200. Compute $\hat{Z}$ = $n/(n+\hat{k})$ and the EB credibility premium P = $\hat{Z} \bar{X} + (1 - \hat{Z})\hat{\mu}$.
worked_example.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Form $\hat{Z}$ from n and $\hat{k}$ before mixing $\bar{X}$ with $\hat{\mu}$.

steps.label: Estimated credibility factor
steps.explanation: Empirical Bayes plugs estimated structurals into the same Bühlmann Z formula.

steps.label: EB premium
steps.explanation: The premium uses estimated μ and k in place of known prior structurals.

steps.label: What makes it Empirical Bayes
steps.explanation: EB estimates structural parameters from collective portfolio data rather than taking them as known from a fully specified prior.
steps.calculation: $\hat{\mu}$, $\hat{k}$ from collective data (not a fully specified prior)

worked_example.common_pitfall: Treating $\hat{\mu}$ and $\hat{k}$ as if they were known prior structurals (fully Bayesian), or using Z = $\hat{k}/(n+\hat{k})$.
